name: Figma
thesis: Figma gives everyone free eyes on the file and charges the moment someone wants to change it. The growth its evidence shows is that seat expansion inside paying accounts, not the virality its filings credit.

sections.summary: Who shows up, from packaging and two migration accounts.

sections.title: Jobs To Be Done

sections.title: The Product
sections.summary: The objects, the actions, and a 2019 look under the hood.

sections.title: Growth Loops
sections.summary: Evidence-bounded: one of five transitions is established.

sections.title: Moats
sections.summary: No defensibility mechanism established from available evidence.

problem.beforeState: By Figma's own 2015 account, designers worked in single-player desktop tools while engineers had collaborative workflows, and design work moved between separate tools for creating, commenting, sharing and storage. No independent pre-2015 source corroborates this characterisation.
problem.afterState: Figma's stated proposition was design software that is online, real-time and collaborative, reached through a browser link with nothing to install. This describes the company's stated intent at launch, not a measured change in how teams worked.
problem.wedge: A browser-based design tool reachable by URL, with simultaneous multiplayer editing announced as arriving in 2016 rather than present at the December 2015 preview release.

whyNow.change: WebGL made GPU-accelerated rendering viable inside the browser, demonstrated to the founders in April 2011.
whyNow.argument: Browser-based creative tooling was blocked on rendering performance rather than on demand. WebGL removed that constraint, which is why the founding demonstration was a graphics demo rather than a collaboration prototype.

segments.name: Product design teams
segments.description: Designers working in shared files, often distributed across offices and time zones, maintaining a common component library. The seat structure and two first hand migration accounts both point here.

segments.name: Developers building from designs
segments.description: Engineers who inspect and hand off from design files. Figma sells them their own Dev seat, which is the clearest signal that they are a distinct paying group.

segments.name: Reviewers and stakeholders
segments.description: Product managers, marketers and clients who look and comment on free View seats without editing. Their existence is documented; their number is not.

powerUser.profile: A distributed design team that keeps a shared design system as published libraries and works in one live file across locations. Both migration accounts describe exactly this shape of team.
behaviours: Publishes and maintains a team component library
Works in the same file across cities and time zones
Hands off to developers through inspect rather than exports
Replaces separate storage and handoff tools with one file

notFor.why: The product is built around a live shared file in a browser. Offline is a reconnect mode, not the main mode, and the collaboration features are the reason teams say they switched. This is an inference from how it is built, not something anyone stated.

jobs.statement: When my design team is spread across offices, help us all work in one live file so we stop juggling versions and handoff tools.

competingAlternatives.name: Sketch plus storage and handoff tools
competingAlternatives.why: The previous setup Intercom describes: a desktop tool wrapped in separate apps for versioning, storage and developer handoff, which they call a messy and limiting ecosystem.

forces.push: Versioned files hidden in folders and a tool ecosystem that had become, in Intercom's words, prohibitively messy and limiting.
forces.pull: A flat document system with no files to save, reachable from a browser by anyone on the team, wherever they sit.
forces.anxiety: Losing Sketch plugins, an unpolished interface, and one to two months of adjustment pain that Intercom reports feeling.
forces.habit: Years of Sketch workflows and libraries, plus the tooling built around them.

jobs.statement: When I maintain a design system, let components be adjusted per instance so I stop building workarounds for rigid overrides.

competingAlternatives.name: Sketch libraries
competingAlternatives.why: Help Scout's system lived in nested Sketch libraries managed through GitHub, with components built to work around Sketch only allowing pre set overrides.

forces.push: Sketch only allowed pre determined overrides, which forced complex nested components as workarounds.
forces.pull: Colour, type and effects can be customised on each instance, so the system gets simpler and stays linked.
forces.anxiety: Rebuilding the whole library by hand. Help Scout retraced components from screenshots and it took about a week.
forces.habit: An established, documented system already in use across live projects.

coreActions: Edit a shared file with others
Inspect a design in Dev Mode
product.atomicUnitOfValue: A live design file, reachable by link, that several people can look at and edit at once.

ahaMoment.description: Opening a colleague's file by link and realising there is no file to download, version or send. Intercom calls this the absence of files.
ahaMoment.trigger: First shared link opened in the browser

businessModel.valueMetric: The paid seat, in four types with role-gated product access; AI credits add a metered consumption element from March 2026.

revenueLines.name: Seat subscriptions
revenueLines.description: Annual or monthly per-seat subscriptions across Professional, Organization and Enterprise plans. The 10-K discloses no revenue split by plan or seat type, so this single line carries all disclosed revenue.

tiers.name: Starter
gates: Free entry tier with unlimited drafts and capped AI credits

tiers.name: Professional
gates: Full product access per seat type
tiers.priceNote: Full $16 / Dev $12 / Collab $3 per seat per month, as of 2026-08-30

tiers.name: Organization
tiers.priceNote: Full $55 / Dev $25 / Collab $5 per seat per month, as of 2026-08-30

tiers.name: Enterprise
gates: Enterprise controls, compliance and dedicated workspaces
tiers.priceNote: Full $90 / Dev $35 / Collab $5 per seat per month, as of 2026-08-30

businessModel.monetizationMoment: The move from free viewing and commenting to a paid seat: granting edit access assigns a billed seat, and where the seat type is unavailable it is added to the subscription under configurable, optionally automatic approval.
businessModel.unitEconomicsShape: Gross margin in the low eighties and falling year over year, with cost of revenue growing far faster than revenue and the company itself forecasting further AI-driven margin compression. Expansion revenue within existing accounts, not new-logo acquisition, is the evidenced growth engine.

brief.grows: Free viewers inside a paying account get edit access and become billed seats, often auto-approved. That expansion, not new-customer virality, is the engine the evidence shows.
brief.earns: Per-seat subscriptions across four seat types, from a free View seat up to $90 a month for a Full seat on Enterprise, with AI credits metered on top since March 2026.
brief.tradeoff: It is funding AI heavily and said so in its 10-K: gross margin fell from 88.3% to 82.4% in a year, and Figma expects AI to push it lower still.
brief.unverified: Whether people who view Figma files for free ever become new paying customers, rather than new seats in accounts that already pay.

verdict.thesis: Figma gives everyone free eyes on the file and charges the moment someone wants to change it. The growth its evidence shows is that seat expansion inside paying accounts, not the virality its filings credit.

getRight.claim: Every free viewer is a paid seat in waiting
getRight.argument: The View seat is free and carries view and comment access, and granting edit access adds a billed seat under approval rules that can be automatic. Reviewers cost nothing to invite and convert without a sales conversation.

getRight.claim: It told investors what the AI bet would cost
getRight.argument: The 10-K states that inference costs will weigh on gross and operating margins, and gross margin moved from 88.3% to 82.4% in the same year. A company naming the price of its own bet in advance is rarer than it should be.

getRight.claim: Expansion inside large accounts is working
getRight.argument: Net dollar retention of 136% on customers above $10,000 a year, and 34% growth in that group, say existing accounts keep buying more. That is the most solid growth evidence in the teardown.

getWrong.claim: Seat upgrades that surprise the person paying
getWrong.argument: Practitioners across 2021 to 2025 describe edit access turning into charges an admin did not notice. Expansion that works because nobody notices is expansion that erodes trust with the person who renews.

getWrong.claim: Its retention metric covers about 2% of customers
getWrong.argument: Net dollar retention is measured only on the 15,964 customers above $10,000, out of roughly 690,000 paying. The headline number says nothing about the 98% below that line.

getWrong.claim: The growth story it tells is not the one it can show
getWrong.argument: The filings credit product virality inherent to the platform. A dedicated search found no mechanism behind that claim, and one well-evidenced mechanism that works inside accounts that already pay.

whatIdDoNext.move: Make seat upgrades visible to whoever pays
whatIdDoNext.rationale: Show the cost at the moment edit access is granted, and send billing admins a monthly digest of seat changes. It turns the most repeated practitioner complaint into a reason to trust the bill.
whatIdDoNext.risk: Fewer silent upgrades means slower expansion revenue at first, and the retention headline may dip before the trust pays back.

whatIdDoNext.rationale: Report net dollar retention for the whole base, or at least for the tier below $10,000, so the expansion story covers the customers it currently leaves out.
whatIdDoNext.risk: If small accounts churn heavily the number will be well below 136%. That is the point of publishing it, and also the danger.

whatIdDoNext.move: Price AI where the cost actually sits
whatIdDoNext.rationale: Credits already meter AI. Tie the allowance to the seats and features that generate inference cost, so margin tracks usage instead of being spread across every seat.
whatIdDoNext.risk: Heavy AI users will see a price rise, and Figma's own filings name AI-native design tools as the place those users could go.

openQuestions: Do people who view a Figma file for free ever become new paying customers, rather than new seats in existing ones?
Has any organisation tried to leave Figma, and what did it cost them?
Do the documented limits of the 2019 multiplayer architecture still hold?
What is retention like for the 98% of paying customers below the $10K line?

interview.question: How does Figma make money from people who never pay?
outline: The View seat is free and includes commenting, so reviewers cost nothing to invite
Granting edit access adds a billed seat, and approval can be automatic
So every reviewer is a latent seat inside an account that already pays
The risk is surprise billing, which practitioners have reported for years

interview.question: Figma's 10-K credits product virality for its growth. How would you test that claim?
outline: Define the chain: a file is shared, a non-user opens it, creates an account, and later pays
Name the missing measurement: viewer to new paying account, as distinct from viewer to new seat
Propose the metric: share of new paying accounts whose first user arrived through a shared link
Contrast with what is evidenced: expansion inside existing accounts, at 136% net dollar retention

interview.question: Gross margin fell from 88% to 82% in a year. As the PM for AI, what do you do?
outline: Separate inference cost from the rest of cost of revenue
Price credits against usage rather than spreading AI across every seat
Keep only the AI features that move retention or expansion enough to pay for themselves
Weigh the competitive risk: the 10-K names AI-native design tools as threats

interview.question: What makes Figma hard to replace?
outline: Be honest: the evidence establishes no moat mechanism yet
Candidates are collaboration, shared libraries and the plugin ecosystem
For each, say what would prove it: a switching cost with a measured consequence
Market position, such as the CMA's 2023 finding, is where it stands, not why it can't be moved

patterns.note: Viewing is free. The moment a viewer is given edit access, a billed seat is added to the account.
The Community catalogue is public with a Remix button; whether it brings in new customers is unestablished.
